items.title: India's little-known minority - The Siddi and the Olympic dream | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Nimeksha Siddi is 18 years old and India's sprinting hope for the 2028 Olympics. Nimeksha belongs to the Siddi ethnic group, whose daily lives are marked by racism and exclusion.

The 18-year-old sprinter Nimeksha flies down the home straight like a bolt of lightning. She's a Siddi. Hardly anyone knows about her people, not even in India, where the Siddi have lived for 500 years. Her ancestors came to India from Africa as slaves or mercenaries. It's not known how many Siddi live in India. They all have the surname Siddi. They are Muslim, Christian or Hindu - and are often mistaken for tourists by many Indians. Most live in poverty, scraping by as day laborers, gathering plants, honey or rubber.

In 1983, India's Minister for Sport launched a program aimed at tapping into the community's athletic potential. Children from Siddi villages were recruited and coached in running. One of the most successful was Kamala Siddi. At the age of 15, she set a national record in the pentathlon, won bronze and gold at international level, and was rewarded with a job on the railways and a flat with running water.

Now her daughter Nimeksha is in the spotlight. She could become India's hope for the 2028 Olympic Games.

items.title: How dependent is Germany on skilled workers from abroad? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>To what extent do German hospitals rely on foreign healthcare professionals? This film looks at expert opinions and the personal experiences of doctors from abroad, to highlight the structural challenges facing the German hospital system.

Germany is training more doctors than ever before - but the shortfall in hospitals still runs to thousands. The reason for this lies less in the absolute figures than in their distribution. Many specialists are drawn to urban centers, while rural areas face a shortage of skilled staff. Furthermore, many doctors are set to retire in the coming years, and an increasing number of them are working part-time. This is creating a noticeable shortage despite the high density of doctors, a problem exacerbated by a hospital system that's under financial pressure in many places. 
Although Germany has many hospitals by international standards, these include numerous small clinics in rural areas that are often barely profitable. To counteract this trend, a comprehensive hospital reform was launched at the end of 2024: fewer sites, greater specialization, and more outpatient treatment. While the Joint Federal Committee sees opportunities for greater efficiency in this move, the German Hospital Association warns that new gaps in care could arise in rural areas.
The documentary follows Mohamed Cherbagi, an internist from Syria who most recently worked at a hospital in Freiberg, Saxony, and Ina Viaroukina from Belarus, a junior doctor at the Harzklinikum in Quedlinburg. Both are taking on roles in places where their German colleagues are becoming increasingly hard to find. Through their personal stories, along with insightful commentary from experts, the documentary shows just how dependent many hospitals are on doctors from abroad, and how this dependence is linked to the structural challenges facing the German hospital system.

items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub
http://gotopia.tech/bookclub

Check out more here:
https://gotopia.tech/episodes/454

Will Briggs - Professor of Computer Science at University of Lynchburg & Author of "C++26 for Lazy Programmers"
Todd L. Montgomery - Software Professional & Advisor at DRW & Co-Author & Co-Maintainer of Aeron, Agrona & Simple Binary Encoding (SBE) 

RESOURCES
Will
https://www.linkedin.com/in/will-briggs-32635714a
https://www.lynchburg.edu/will-briggs

Todd
https://twitter.com/toddlmontgomery
https://www.linkedin.com/in/todd-montgomery-413a3216
https://github.com/tmontgomery

DESCRIPTION
Will Briggs — a University of Lynchburg computer science professor with three decades of experience teaching C++ — joins Todd L. Montgomery to talk through C++26 for Lazy Programmers, and the conversation opens on the question every language-learning book has to answer right now: does learning a language still matter when AI writes so much of the code?
Briggs' answer is refreshingly unhyped — he tests a new AI tool about once a year on a real, medium-difficulty problem, and as of this year's attempt, it still couldn't solve one, though it's genuinely useful for speeding up work he already understands. Both he and Montgomery land on the same practical conclusion: reading code fluently matters more now, not less, because code is increasingly how AI communicates back to you, and you can't debug or direct what you can't read. The rest of the conversation is a genuine craft discussion about how to teach C++ well — sequencing concepts so a beginner never has to hold two new ideas at once, giving double duty to topics like operator overloading and custom string classes, and deliberately introducing pointers nineteen chapters before ever using the word "pointer", by building the underlying mental model through arrays first.

For engineers who've been away from C++ or are watching it from a distance, there are a few sharp, specific takeaways: Briggs points to AI-generated C++ as noticeably more reliable than AI-generated Java, plausibly because of training-corpus quality rather than anything about the language itself, and he's blunt about C++26's biggest usability problem being proliferation, not power — he cites a case of 25 different ways floating around online just to initialize a single number, and argues the language needs fewer new ways to do old things. He also makes a case, backed by the TIOBE index, that C — a language from 1972 — is still the second most popular language in the world, and that learning C++ specifically (precisely because it's hard and concept-dense) is some of the best preparation available for picking up nearly any other language quickly afterward.

DESCRIPTION
Kaspar von Grünberg and Luca Galante — co-authors of the new book Thinking in Platforms and co-founders of Humanitec and the PlatformEngineering.org community — trace their field back to an origin story most engineers will recognize: a company held hostage by a single backend engineer who could threaten to walk unless he got a 3x raise. That "key person dependency" problem, they argue, is exactly what industrialization solved a century earlier when Henry Ford moved manufacturing from artisan workshops to standardized assembly lines — and it's the same move platform engineering makes for software: treating the internal setup as a product instead of something that "just happens" to a team. The book is structured in three parts — historical foundations, a "path-to-outcome" conceptual framework built around golden paths, and a hands-on playbook for going from a minimum viable platform to full enterprise adoption — because, as they note, most platform efforts don't fail on the technical side; they fail on the social side, in getting buy-in from developers, executives, and security teams alike.

The conversation's sharpest point for engineers building with AI right now: agents make platforms non-optional, not less necessary. An AI agent dropped into an enterprise full of undocumented "tribal knowledge" fails for the same reason a new hire would — except at scale, and fast. Von Grünberg's analogy: it's like hiring a brilliant intern and sending them into an office where nobody speaks their language, then being surprised there's no output a week later. That means real infrastructure — context management, security, observability, governance — has to exist before agents can be productive, and the old rule of thumb that you needed 100+ developers to justify a platform team no longer applies when a single person can be running a thousand agents. The bigger claim: platform engineering is already spreading past IT into security, data, and eventually every knowledge-work function, becoming less a software discipline and more the operating model for AI-first organizations.

In November 2002, the oil tanker “Prestige” sank off the coast of Galicia in northwestern Spain after encountering a winter storm, causing one of the worst oil spills in the country’s history.

The tanker had a murky and complicated backstory — making it difficult to track culpability. At 26 years old, the rusting, single-hulled tanker was well past the age of retirement. But that didn’t deter the owners from loading the aging ship with crude oil number 4, one of the most toxic fuel oils known.

After the spill, Spain imposed a six-month ban on fishing in the region, leading to great economic hardship.

“Spain: The Lawless Sea” investigated what went wrong with the tanker and uncovered a largely unregulated maritime system that offered few safeguards against environmental disasters.

“This is an act of terror, a criminal act,” said Rafael Mouzo, a fisherman and then-mayor of the coastal town of Concurbion. “We need an international tribunal to judge ... all those responsible for the spill.”

<article>Jonathan Halliwell explains how quantum decoherence is key to understanding how we transition from a world with a wave-like nature of matter and energy to the classical macroscopic world that we’re used to.

“The Joy of Why” is a Quanta Magazine podcast about curiosity and the pursuit of knowledge. The mathematician and author Steven Strogatz and the cosmologist and author Janna Levin take turns interviewing leading researchers about the great scientific and mathematical questions of our time. ---------

Quantum mechanics may be one of the most precisely tested paradigms in science, but there’s still no universally accepted interpretation of what it tells us about reality. How do we get from the wave-like behavior of quantum systems to the solid, macroscopic world of objects and the universe at large?

Jonathan Halliwell, a professor of theoretical physics at Imperial College London, has spent his career probing the foundations of quantum theory. In this episode, he tells Steven Strogatz why decoherence — the process by which fragile quantum behavior becomes dispersed through interactions with the surrounding environment — is key to the transition from quantum to classical behavior, and he describes the “histories” approach that he uses to understand this. Along the way, Halliwell tackles some of the field’s deepest paradoxes. He explains why the quantum-to-classical transition doesn’t require a conscious observer, and he explores Einstein’s famous question of whether the moon is really there when no one looks. The conversation ends with Halliwell explaining how yoga and meditation help him sit with the mystery of competing perspectives in science.

items.title: Storms, waves and risky maneuvers - The most dangerous job in the North Sea? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Marine pilots must make crucial decisions under extreme conditions. Transferring from a cargo ship to a small pilot boat in hurricane-force gusts can be fatal.

For marine pilots, this is the most dangerous moment in their daily working lives: climbing down a rope ladder from a cargo ship in gale-force gusts, and transferring to a small pilot boat. In mid-January, a pilot fell into the sea off Borkum and was taken to hospital suffering from hypothermia. Just a few days earlier, a British colleague died during a similar maneuver.

Harbor pilot Gerhard Janssen and sea pilot Dominik Thieben are getting ready for their assignment. In force 8 winds, they set off in the pilot boat to the cargo ship "Silver Soul". They must guide it safely out of the harbor, along the Ems River in northern Germany, and out into the North Sea. They face oncoming traffic, poor visibility and a narrow channel that leaves little room to maneuver. Off the island of Borkum, a pilot boat will pick them up and take them back to shore. Transferring vessels in a storm can be fatal.

Whether the ship can sail at all depends on the waves. Otherwise, the pilots will have to be picked up by helicopter, which can withstand winds of up to force 11 on the Beaufort scale. This corresponds to a hurricane-force storm, with winds of over 100 kilometers per hour. The pilots are hauled into the helicopter by a rope. With every maneuver, the pilots and crew -- both on the pilot boats and in the helicopter -- must decide how much risk they are prepared to take.

items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>An increasing number of people don't want to be cremated or buried after their death. They want their bodies to return to the earth as fertile soil. This poses both an ethical and a legal challenge.

In Europe, committed citizens are campaigning to have 'humusation' - the composting of human remains - scientifically investigated, validated and legalized. In the US, this alternative to cremation and burial is already practiced in two states. The idea is culturally radical but based on a natural process. Called ‘aerobic decomposition,’ it has been perfected by nature over millions of years.

Gradually, a movement is emerging that was long regarded as marginal and controversial. Its pioneers are breaking taboos, raising environmental awareness and challenging the funeral industry. Through what's known as 're-burial', they're shaping a different understanding of death - as part of a cycle that renews life - thereby paving the way for new rites.

<article>How record-breaking distance runner Lornah Kiplagat helped other women in Kenya break social barriers and train to be professional runners. (Aired March 2004)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

For decades, Kenyan men had ranked among the world’s best long distance runners — bringing home one Olympic medal after another and sweeping marathons from coast to coast in the U.S. Largely confined to traditional roles at home and on the farm, most Kenyan women had only watched from the sidelines. But when Lornah Kiplagat emerged from the highlands of northwest Kenya as one of the best female runners in the world in the late 1990s and early 2000s, she committed herself and her prize money to building what was then the first women’s running camp in the country.

In “Kenya: Run, Lornah, Run,” FRONTLINE/World correspondents Alexis Bloom and Cassandra Herrman documented Kiplagat’s journey, met emerging female athletes at her unique camp, and learned about how they were breaking social expectations in a country that largely prescribed traditional, domestic roles for women.
As Kiplagat noted in the documentary, “At the end, it’s not only about running. It’s a way of changing the whole lifestyle of women in Kenya.” 

In the two decades since “Run, Lornah, Run” aired, Kiplagat’s camp, the High Altitude Training Center, has become a destination for elite runners — both female and male — from around the world. Kiplagat, now a citizen of the Netherlands, continues to support young women in Kenya through programming at the center and through her eponymous foundation.

items.author: History Hit
items.content:
<article>History Hit's Dan Snow dives on the incredibly well-preserved remains of the 18th-century warship. 

Complete with cannons, muskets and coils of rope, it's a discovery that's rewriting our understanding of the evolution of the Royal Navy. 

The special film sees Dan on a personal mission to restore HMS Northumberland to her rightful place in the story of the Royal Navy, as one of the most iconic and important ships, the missing link between the Mary Rose and HMS Victory. Together with a team of leading experts, he'll be investigating the ship’s construction, her pivotal role in the Royal Navy‘s search for the perfect warship, and the circumstances surrounding her tragic loss.

The Great Storm of 1703 was one of the deadliest maritime disasters in history. A night of terror that cost the lives of over 1000 sailors and thirteen of the Royal Navy’s most valuable ships. Tearing across the English Channel, swallowing ships, shattering cities, and claiming thousands of lives. Amongst the storm's casualties was Northumberland, one of the Royal Navy's most formidable warships, sunk with all hands.

Lost to the sea for over three hundred years. Shifting sands have started to reveal the broken vessel, once the pride of Her Majesty’s Fleet. But now, exposed to the elements, archaeologists are racing against time to save as much of the ship as possible before it’s gone forever.

items.title: From neo-nazi to soccer coach for refugees | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>A former far-right extremist now coaches a soccer team of young refugees. As a coach and mentor, he helps them build a sense of community and settle into their new home.

Thomas Eichstätt, known to everyone as "Eichi,” used to be deeply involved in the far-right scene in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Today, he volunteers in the small town of Torgelow as the coach of FC Pio. 
Many of the young players he coaches have fled their home countries. They face an array of challenges in their adopted country: they must find jobs, navigate a lack of acceptance, and process their experiences as refugees.
But on the field, what matters most is the moment. Soccer offers these players structure and a sense of belonging. 
Off the field, many are caught up in the difficult process of integration and are consumed by a longing for home. Whether on the field or off of it, "Eichi” is there for them. For some players, he has become an important role model.
At the same time, the soccer coach is coming to terms with his own past. "I used to be a bad person,” says Eichstätt, of his time in the far-right scene. He receives no payment for his work with FC Pio—the financially strapped municipality can’t afford to fund his efforts.
Loraine Blumenthal’s film shows how soccer and personal commitment can build bridges—even in an environment characterized by frequent political demands for deportation.

Germany just freed up half a trillion euros to rebuild itself — and eighteen months later, the money has barely moved. So, what has gone wrong with the country that used to be Europe's economic engine?

items.content:
<article>On September 11th, 2001, four hijacked airplanes struck the heart of America. At 8:46 am, New York time, the first airplane crashed into the World Trade Centre -- an attack whose global consequences still reverberate to this day.

As early as 1999, Osama bin Laden devised a plan to use civilian aircraft as weapons. The targets were chosen for their symbolic significance to the USA: The World Trade Centre was an economic hub, the Pentagon was the military nerve center, and the White House was the center of political power.
But how could the attack manage to succeed? Months before the attacks, the CIA had crucial leads - including the names of known terrorists. Yet they failed to put the puzzle together.
This documentary retraces the attacks of September 11th, 2001 in precise chronological order - in the air, at Ground Zero, in newsrooms and in the centers of power in the USA.  Archival footage, audio recordings and findings from the 9/11 Commission Report make it possible to reconstruct the events, almost in real time.
"9/11 - The Day that Changed the World" is a sober analysis of a global turning point: it examines missed warnings, the chaos of the day and the impact of a moment that reshaped the world.

items.content:
<article>Airing just two days after 9/11, this documentary offered vital context on U.S. efforts to track Osama bin Laden, his terrorist network and his role in earlier attacks on Americans. (Aired 2001)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

In the hours after 9/11 — the worst terror attack on the U.S. in history — the CIA and FBI briefed political leaders in Washington, D.C. that their search for the terrorists responsible was focusing on one name above all others: Osama bin Laden. 

With opening and closing commentary from legendary journalist Bill Moyers, FRONTLINE’s “Hunting bin Laden,” which aired two days after the 9/11 attacks, captured the shock, grief and horror that gripped the U.S. when the twin towers fell — and documented the emergence of one central question: Why did U.S. intelligence agencies fail so tragically to “connect the dots” and uncover this enormous operation in time?

Built on an investigation into bin Laden and his militant Islamist network that FRONTLINE had aired two years earlier, and featuring new interviews conducted in the hours after 9/11, “Hunting bin Laden” was a collaboration with The New York Times. Director and producer Martin Smith and correspondent Lowell Bergman pieced together how bin Laden, a wealthy Saudi Arabian exile then believed to be hiding in Afghanistan, had eluded the U.S. while building a terror network and calling for the killing of Americans.

The documentary traced how the U.S. responded when bin Laden’s ideology emerged in connection with several major acts of Islamist terrorism against Americans in the 90s — from the 1993 attack on the World Trade Center, to the bombings of U.S. military installations in Saudi Arabia, to the 1998 bombings of U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania. It also raised tough questions about the evidence used to justify Washington’s retaliatory missile strikes in Sudan, a country where bin Laden was once based, following those embassy bombings. 

At the time “Hunting bin Laden” aired, the search for survivors in the wake of the 9/11 attacks was ongoing. As Moyers noted, a connection between bin Laden and the attacks had yet to be officially established.

“How do we bring the guilty to justice without making martyrs of them? And can we distinguish between those who commit the crimes and the innocent who share their culture but not their cause?” Moyers asked. “Not only our security as a nation is at stake, but our values as a people.”

“Hunting Bin Laden” was a FRONTLINE co-production with The New York Times and Rain Media, Inc. It was produced and directed by Martin Smith. It was written by Martin Smith and Lowell Bergman. items.title: Osteoarthritis - New hope for the knee | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Cold therapy, knee distraction or cartilage transplantation from the nose to the knee: what really helps with knee pain? New procedures are bringing fresh hope to people with osteoarthritis and joint degeneration.

Knee pain, wear and tear, osteoarthritis: millions of people suffer from these conditions. Natural remedies and high-tech medicine can alleviate the symptoms and improve joint mobility.  

Cartilage loss in the knee was long considered irreversible. The cartilage acts as a shock absorber between the bones of the joint and cushions the impact of each step. Once it starts wearing away, the bones rub against one another. This can lead to osteoarthritis; often accompanied by pain and restricted movement.

This is where an innovative approach from The Netherlands comes in: knee joint distraction. When the bones of the knee joint are pulled slightly apart, this creates a space that stimulates the body's natural cartilage-repair mechanisms. In Germany, orthopedic surgeon Kaywan Izadpanah from the University Medical Centre Freiburg is one of the first doctors to perform this procedure.

Researchers at Basel University Hospital are trying something else. They remove a small piece of tissue from the nasal septum of patients, cultivate the cells in the laboratory, and then transplant the cultured tissue into damaged areas of the knee joint. The procedure aims to repair cartilage damage and improve joint function.

For mild knee and joint pain, non-surgical remedies are an option. The "Rostock Seals” swear by the power of cold-water therapy: the swimming club’s members find renewed vitality through ice bathing in the wintery Baltic Sea. Some take it a step further, utilizing a cryotherapy chamber set at minus 110 degrees. They report immediate relief from their symptoms and an improved sense of well-being.
